analysis.one_liner: Bans individual stock ownership by the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, and top federal officials.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2023 with sponsorship from one Democrat and one Republican, the bill never got a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the President, the Vice President, Members of Congress, and their spouses and dependent children from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, and similar investments, requiring them to sell any such holdings within 180 days. It would apply the same ban to senior executive branch officials, including Senior Executive Service employees and generals and admirals at the O-7 pay grade and above. It would also require officials to report any federal contracts, grants, or loans they or their families apply for or receive, add automatic fines for late financial disclosure filings, and put disclosure forms in searchable online databases the public can download.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer have officials making policy decisions while holding personal stakes in the companies those decisions affect. The bill also increases public visibility of officials' finances, including federal payments to their families.

how_it_helps.text: Bans covered officials from holding or trading individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, and derivatives; only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury securities remain allowed [S2].
Requires divestiture within 180 days and keeps the ban in effect for 180 days after an official leaves service [S2].

Requires officials to report, within 30 to 45 days, any application for or receipt of federal payments including loans, contracts, and grants by themselves, their spouses, dependent children, or businesses they control [S2].
Imposes automatic $500 fines for late transaction reports under the STOCK Act and requires profits from prohibited trades to be disgorged to the Treasury [S2].
Requires Members of Congress and senior executive officials' disclosure reports to be posted in searchable, downloadable online databases with API access [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, and senior executive branch officials, who would have to sell individual stock holdings within 180 days and could no longer trade individual securities, serve on corporate boards, or hold net short positions. Their families' holdings are covered too.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and top officials

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is modest for executive branch officials: the automatic fine is capped at $10,000 or the amount earned in the violation, whichever is greater, which is small relative to the wealth of many covered officials [S2].
Officials could still hold diversified mutual funds and ETFs, so they could keep broad market exposure, including to sectors their policies affect, as long as the holdings are diversified [S2].

A good-faith objection to any ownership ban is that it could complicate recruiting experienced people with private-sector assets into senior government roles, and compliance logistics (like unvested equity) would depend on ethics-office guidance the bill leaves to regulators [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is removing personal financial stakes from policy decisions by the people who make them — a structural fix rather than a pocketbook transfer. The costs fall on a narrow group (senior officials and their families) and are mostly about giving up individual stock trading, since diversified funds and Treasuries remain available. The main weakness is enforcement teeth, particularly the modest executive-branch fine, but the ban itself is straightforward and enforceable on paper. The trade favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, joined by Sen. Josh Hawley [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day [S4].
One Republican signed on as a cosponsor, making the bill bipartisan at introduction [S3].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and the senior executive branch officials the bill covered are better off: they can continue holding and trading individual stocks and keeping those holdings in their families, and they face no new federal-payment reporting requirements or late-filing fines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The officials the bill would have restricted

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Stock Trading for Government Officials Act of 2023

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: Original Republican cosponsor, joined at introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship; one additional Republican cosponsored later

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 25, 2023 and never scheduled a markup, hearing vote, or committee vote; the bill sat there until the Congress ended

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the 18 months after referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican as original cosponsor and drew one more Republican cosponsor, but because no committee or floor vote ever happened, there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill would have required them to sell individual stocks within 180 days, banned them and their spouses and dependent children from trading individual securities, serving on corporate boards, or holding net short positions, and imposed fines of at least 10 percent of the value of violating trades. This is the concentrated interest the bill targeted, and the bill's death leaves the current rules — disclosure-based, with no ownership ban — in place.

industries.industry: Senior executive branch officials (Senior Executive Service, generals and admirals O-7+, the President and Vice President)
industries.note: They would face the same ownership ban with a 180-day divestiture window, plus disgorgement of violating profits and fines up to $10,000 or the amount earned in the violation. The bill would also have required reporting of federal contracts, grants, and loans sought or received by them or their families.

industries.industry: Brokerage and wealth-management firms serving federal officials
industries.note: Officials covered by the ban would have had to move out of individual securities and could remain only in diversified funds and Treasuries, shrinking the individual-stock business these firms do with officials. Public interest and this industry's interest in the bill run in the same direction, though the effect on the industry is modest.
